hops.title: Regent honeyeaters singing other species' songs
hops.text: In 2021, Ross Crates and colleagues cited an estimate of only 200 to 400 wild regent honeyeaters, scattered across 300,000 square kilometers of southeastern Australia. Fathers stop singing while raising chicks and chase independent youngsters away, so a young male has to find other adult males to copy. The team classified the songs of 146 wild males. About 27 percent strayed from the regional norm, and 18 birds sang no regent honeyeater song at all; instead, their songs resembled other species, such as little wattlebirds, noisy friarbirds and pied currawongs. Males whose songs strayed from the norm were significantly less likely to have found a mate.

sources.citation: Crates et al., Proc. R. Soc. B 288:20210225 (2021)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A black-and-yellow regent honeyeater singing on a eucalyptus branch while a gray friarbird listens from a nearby branch.
image.caption: Some regent honeyeaters sing like other species, possibly from scarce tutors, and males with atypical songs pair less often.

hops.title: Barn owls in prism glasses
hops.text: Eric Knudsen fitted young barn owls with tiny prism spectacles that shifted their view sideways. The juveniles' brains remapped where sounds belong, so that hearing lined up again with the shifted scene. Adults wearing prisms for the first time adjusted very little to the same large shift in the usual tests. In 1998, adults that had adapted to a large prism shift as juveniles could adapt to that same shift again. Knudsen concluded that early learning left an enduring trace in the circuit. Four years later, Brie Linkenhoker and Knudsen found that even naive adult owls could remap when the shift arrived in small steps rather than one jump.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A barn owl wearing tiny prism spectacles on a perch, tilting its head toward a small speaker.
image.caption: Adult owls can relearn a prism shift they learned when young, or learn a new one in small steps.

hops.afterHeading: Language: what the age effects do and do not show
hops.title: The puffless t in "star"
hops.text: Hold your palm an inch from your mouth and say "top," then "star." On "top," a puff of air hits your hand. On "star," the t that follows the s barely puffs at all. English treats both sounds as versions of the same consonant, t. In a 1997 lab study, Pegg and Werker compared a syllable starting with that puffless t, with no s in front, to one starting with d. English-speaking adults rated the two as equally good examples of "da." In their listening test, 11 of 20 six- to eight-month-olds met the criterion for telling them apart; only 1 of 12 ten- to twelve-month-olds did.

sources.citation: Pegg & Werker, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 102:3742-3753 (1997)
Kazanina, Bowers & Idsardi, Psychon. Bull. Rev. 25:560-585 (2018)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A college student at a desk holding an open hand in front of their mouth with a surprised expression.
image.caption: In the test, 11 of 20 6-to-8-month-olds reached criterion for telling puffless t from d, versus 1 of 12 10-to-12-month-olds.
